strengths: The problem is important and well motivated: stochastic, scene-wide trajectory forecasting is a useful representation of uncertainty about future motion.
The method achieves substantial reported gains over ATM and Tra-MoE on LIBERO, including single-sample comparisons, so these improvements are not merely benefits of best-of-K selection.

The evaluation includes several datasets, adapted trajectory baselines, fine-tuned video generators, a controlled output-modality experiment, and a human preference study. Ablations examine latent modeling, model size, and training with estimated trajectories.
The appendix provides substantial architectural and training detail, and the reported inference costs suggest practical benefits over video-generation pipelines.
weaknesses: The central claim that RGB generation overhead causes inferior motion modeling is not established. Video methods incur an additional tracking stage, and Table 21 shows substantial discrepancies even when CoTracker processes ground-truth videos: conditional FVMD increases from 8979.95 to 21331.69. Although this experiment uses a different sample count from the main evaluation, it directly undermines the assertion that tracking artifacts have been ruled out. High RGB reconstruction quality and standard tracking accuracy do not resolve this confound.

Reported results contain material unexplained inconsistencies. Ours (L) has in-distribution FVMD 13745 and LRTL 14.1 in Table 3, versus 6470.3 and 6.4 in Table 11. Table 4's Ours (L) out-of-distribution results nearly duplicate Table 6's in-distribution trajectory results, which Table 12 attributes to Ours (B). The text also says all metrics worsen out of distribution, contrary to several table entries. These discrepancies require reconciliation before the quantitative conclusions are reliable.

Novelty is primarily architectural integration: stochastic trajectory generation already exists in Track2Act, while the VAE, flow matching, and factorized transformer components are established. Missing matched-backbone deterministic and sparse-versus-dense ablations prevent attributing improvements to uncertainty modeling or scene-wide grids. Comparisons also change image encoders and conditioning mechanisms; notably, the adapted Track2Act already predicts the same grid.

The physical-plausibility evidence is limited. Rank-5 reconstruction error is a structural proxy, not a test of rigid-body dynamics: nonrigid low-rank deformations can score well, and perspective projection complicates the rank assumption. No direct collision, interpenetration, or gravitational-consistency tests substantiate the broader physical claims.

Distributional evaluation uses only 16 independent initial scenes per Kubric benchmark, without confidence intervals or repeated-training uncertainty. Best-of-K is insufficiently specified for two sets of futures and cannot alone establish distributional coverage or calibration. The small user study provides supporting preference evidence but does not resolve these limitations.

Real-world support is modest: Physics101 improves overall error from 30.08 to 28.62, loses on two of five scenarios, and evaluates only one sample per condition. Moreover, Table 14 identifies the headline result as the variant without the proposed VAE; the VAE variant scores 31.67. Qualitative Physion transfer examples do not establish broad real-world generalization.

strengths: The problem is well motivated: forecasting a distribution of scene-wide point trajectories is a useful alternative to generating complete videos when motion is the desired output.
The method achieves consistent improvements over ATM and Tra-MoE on LIBERO, including single-sample comparisons in Tables 9–10. The benefits therefore do not depend solely on best-of-K selection.

The experiments include several video generators, fine-tuned baselines, an adapted Track2Act, a controlled output-modality comparison, and ablations of the VAE and model size. Reported inference costs are substantially lower than video generation.
The appendix provides substantial architectural and training details, and the paper explicitly recognizes the complementary limitations of its distributional and low-rank metrics.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited and the attribution of gains is insufficiently established. Track2Act already generates trajectories stochastically; this method combines established latent flow matching, a trajectory VAE, and a Latte-derived transformer. Comparisons simultaneously change image features, conditioning, architecture, and point coverage. Matched deterministic-versus-stochastic and sparse-versus-dense ablations are needed to support the claimed benefits of uncertainty modeling and global scene reasoning.

The central causal claim—that video models fail because generating RGB consumes capacity needed for physical motion—is stronger than the evidence. Table 6 supports the practical advantage of trajectory outputs under the tested setup, but changes latent representations, decoders, and the need for tracking. Good CoTracker performance on real simulator videos and high RGB reconstruction quality do not exclude tracking errors on generated videos or establish the proposed capacity-allocation mechanism.

Physical plausibility is only weakly measured. A small rank-5 reconstruction residual does not establish rigidity, valid collisions, or physical dynamics: coherent non-rigid transformations can also be low rank, and perspective projection complicates the rigidity interpretation. FVMD summarizes motion statistics rather than physical correctness. The user study provides complementary evidence, but lacks uncertainty estimates and a sufficiently explicit sampling protocol.

The strongest distributional evaluation uses only 16 initial scenes per Kubric benchmark. Generating 64 futures per scene does not establish breadth across initial conditions, and confidence intervals or repeated-training results are absent. Best-of-K is described without a precise aggregation formula over generated and simulated futures, leaving its coverage interpretation unclear.

There are substantial unexplained numerical inconsistencies. Table 11 reports in-distribution Ours (L) FVMD of 6470.3 and LRTL of 6.4, versus 13745 and 14.1 in Table 3, without identifying a different evaluation protocol. Section 4.2 also says all metrics increase out of distribution, whereas many values decrease in Table 4. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the reported comparisons.

Real-world support is modest and does not clearly validate the proposed latent method. Physics101 improves overall MSE from 30.08 to 28.62 but loses on two of five scenarios. Table 14 reveals that the headline 28.62 result belongs to the variant without a VAE; the VAE variant scores 31.67, worse than WAN. This distinction is not clear in the main results. Single-sample MSE cannot establish distributional quality, and Physion-to-real transfer is only qualitative.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: predicting multiple plausible scene motions from a single image. Dense trajectory generation is a sensible representation, and the image-conditioned trajectory VAE and flow-matching model form a coherent approach.

LIBERO results show consistent improvements over ATM and Tra-MoE, including average-sample and single-sample comparisons. These gains provide evidence beyond the expected advantage of best-of-K evaluation.

The experiments cover several datasets, adapted trajectory baselines, fine-tuned video generators, and an architecture-controlled comparison of RGB versus trajectory generation. The VAE ablations and experiments with tracker-derived training labels are useful.

Reported inference costs are substantially lower than those of video generators. The appendix provides substantial architecture, training, and baseline-adaptation details, and the user study offers complementary evidence of perceptual plausibility.
weaknesses: The central attribution to RGB-generation overhead remains insufficiently isolated from tracking error. Table 20 evaluates tracking on benchmark videos, which does not establish equivalent accuracy on generated videos. More concerningly, Table 21 shows a substantial metric penalty from tracking real ground-truth videos: scene FVMD rises from approximately 8,980 to 21,332. Although its sample count differs from the main evaluation, this demonstrates that the measurement pipeline itself can materially affect the comparison. The matched-architecture experiment is valuable but retains this asymmetry.

The physical-plausibility and uncertainty evaluations are limited. A low rank-5 reconstruction error is not sufficient to establish rigidity: coherent nonrigid deformations can also be low rank, and perspective projection complicates the interpretation. Best-of-K does not establish distributional calibration or coverage, and its aggregation over the two sets of futures is insufficiently specified. The principal conditional-distribution benchmark contains only 16 distinct scenes, with no confidence intervals or repeated-training results.

The novelty is primarily an integration of existing generative and architectural components. Track2Act already generates stochastic trajectories, and its adaptation here also uses a dense grid. Controlled deterministic-versus-generative and sparse-versus-dense variants of the proposed architecture are missing, so the claimed benefits of uncertainty modeling and scene-wide coverage are not disentangled from stronger image features and other architectural changes.

Real-world evidence is modest. On Physics101, the reported overall improvement over WAN is approximately 4.9%, with worse results in two of five scenarios and no uncertainty estimates. Table 14 reveals that the headline result uses the variant without the VAE; the full VAE variant scores 31.67, worse than WAN's 30.08. Single-sample MSE cannot substantiate the central claim about learning multiple plausible futures.

Several reporting issues reduce confidence in reproducibility. Table 4's Ours (L) results closely match the Base model's in-distribution results in Tables 6 and 12, requiring clarification of model and split assignments. The text also claims that all OOD metrics increase, contrary to the tables. Video-baseline fine-tuning hyperparameters and the exact best-of-K procedure need fuller specification.

strengths: The paper addresses an important forecasting problem with a sensible representation: jointly generating dense point trajectories captures scene context and supports multiple possible futures without synthesizing appearance.

The evaluation is broad, spanning Kubric, LIBERO, Physics101, and Cityscapes. Improvements on LIBERO persist for single samples and averaged predictions, rather than depending solely on best-of-K selection. Cityscapes results show substantial gains over both Track2Act and fine-tuned WAN.

The controlled modality experiments and joint RGB–trajectory generation experiment provide useful evidence that explicit motion representations improve motion forecasting. Ablations additionally examine the VAE, grid density, model scale, noisy supervision, and multiple conditioning frames.

The appendix provides substantial architectural, training, and baseline-adaptation details. Reported inference costs suggest a practically valuable efficiency advantage, and the user study provides complementary perceptual evidence.
weaknesses: The central attribution of video-model errors to RGB-generation overhead is not established. Table 24 shows substantial degradation from tracking genuine ground-truth videos: scene FVMD increases from 8979.95 to 21331.69 and best-of-K from 114.241 to 191.304. Although this experiment uses a different sample count from the main tables, it directly undermines the assertion that tracking artifacts have been ruled out. Training the proposed model on estimated tracks does not isolate errors introduced by tracking baseline outputs. A matched oracle-video comparison and motion evaluation through reconstructed RGB are needed.

The physical-plausibility evidence is limited. Low rank is not sufficient for rigidity: coherent scaling, shearing, and other nonrigid motions can also have low-rank trajectory matrices. Neither LRTL nor histogram-based FVMD establishes valid collisions, nonpenetration, or force propagation. The paper acknowledges some metric limitations, but its claims about learning physical consistency exceed what these proxies demonstrate.

Several reported results require reconciliation. For apparently corresponding Kubric evaluations, Ours (L) has FVMD 13745 in Table 3 but 6470.3 in Table 13, without a clear explanation of the protocol difference. Table 14 also gives different LRTL from Table 3. The claim that all metrics worsen out of distribution contradicts Tables 3–4, where multiple metrics improve. These discrepancies reduce confidence in the quantitative conclusions.

Novelty is primarily the integration of established components: trajectory generation, a conditional VAE, flow matching, and a Latte-derived transformer. Earlier work already generates motion from still images, including Track2Act and Walker et al. The comparison with Track2Act changes image encoding and conditioning substantially; without a strengthened baseline using comparable DINO features and patch-level conditioning, the source of the advantage remains unclear.

The strongest distributional evaluation contains only 16 initial scenes per setting, with no uncertainty estimates for the main comparisons. Best-of-K is described insufficiently precisely and does not establish distributional calibration or mode coverage. The density ablation reports the best score among three checkpoints without clearly identifying an independent selection set.

Real-world support for the full latent-generative formulation is mixed. The Physics101 headline result uses the variant without the VAE; the VAE version scores 31.67 MSE versus WAN's 30.08. Single-sample MSE cannot assess the claimed uncertainty modeling, and synthetic-to-real Physion transfer is qualitative. Overall, the promising empirical contribution is slightly below the acceptance threshold because measurement confounds and reporting inconsistencies leave central claims unresolved.

strengths: The paper presents a useful formulation of single-image motion forecasting: jointly generating dense trajectory grids with an image-conditioned VAE and latent flow matching. This supports multiple plausible futures and scene-wide interactions.

The empirical gains are substantial across several settings. LIBERO improvements persist when evaluating average samples rather than only best-of-K predictions. On Cityscapes, mean MSE improves from 3495.43 for fine-tuned WAN to 1565.06.

The evaluation includes unusually broad comparisons: deterministic trajectory predictors, a retrained Track2Act baseline, pretrained and fine-tuned video generators, synthetic shape generalization, and two real-world datasets.

The appendices provide meaningful ablations of trajectory density, latent modeling, model size, and pseudo-label supervision. The shared-architecture modality comparison and improved RGB motion from joint RGB–trajectory generation offer concrete evidence that explicit trajectory modeling is beneficial.
Architecture, training, baseline adaptations, and evaluation procedures are described extensively. The reported inference speed improvements make the approach practically relevant.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that video generators fail because of RGB-generation overhead is stronger than the evidence. Table 23 measures tracking accuracy on benchmark videos, not on generated videos. Table 24 shows that applying CoTracker to real simulated videos already substantially worsens the distributional metrics. Thus tracking error remains a confound, despite the valuable shared-architecture experiment.

The metrics provide incomplete evidence of physical plausibility and uncertainty modeling. Low rank is not sufficient for rigidity and does not establish correct collisions, gravity, or nonpenetration. Best-of-K matching does not establish distributional coverage or calibration, while velocity-histogram FVMD can miss spatially incorrect interactions.

The main conditional-distribution benchmark contains only 16 initial scenes per setting. Numerous sampled futures do not replace scene diversity, and results lack confidence intervals or repeated training runs. The 20-person preference study uses the same small scene set and best-of-K selection, limiting conclusions about typical generated samples.

The methodological novelty is primarily an effective combination of established components. Prior work already generates trajectories from images. Comparisons also change image encoders and conditioning mechanisms, so a matched deterministic version and matched Track2Act conditioning would better isolate the claimed benefits of stochastic prediction and architectural design.

Some reporting needs reconciliation. Table 6's in-distribution trajectory results nearly duplicate the out-of-distribution results in Table 4, and Table 13 reports markedly different scores without adequately explaining their relationship to the main protocol. The text also says all OOD metrics increase, although many decrease. Physics101's headline result uses the no-VAE variant; the full VAE model has worse overall MSE than WAN (31.67 versus 30.08). These issues weaken confidence in the strongest general claims.

strengths: The paper presents a useful approach to uncertain motion forecasting: image-conditioned generation of scene-wide trajectory grids using a trajectory VAE and flow matching. Its practical contribution is clear despite relying on established components.

Evaluation is unusually broad, covering synthetic physics, robotic manipulation, and real-world motion. Improvements on LIBERO persist under single-sample and average-sample evaluation, and the Cityscapes gains over Track2Act and fine-tuned WAN are substantial.

The fixed-architecture modality comparison is a valuable experiment. Joint RGB-and-trajectory generation also improves motion extracted from generated videos, strengthening the case that explicit trajectory modeling benefits video synthesis.

The appendix provides substantial implementation detail and useful ablations on trajectory density, latent modeling, model size, pseudo-label supervision, and multiple-frame conditioning. Reported inference costs demonstrate a meaningful practical advantage.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily in the combination and empirical investigation. Stochastic trajectory prediction from images predates this work, including Walker et al. and Track2Act. The paper should narrow its novelty claims and distinguish its contribution more precisely from these predecessors.

The conclusion that RGB-generation overhead causes motion failures is stronger than the evidence. Good tracking accuracy on ground-truth videos does not establish tracking reliability on generated videos. Table 24 itself shows substantial metric degradation from applying CoTracker to real simulator outputs. The controlled experiments support a representation advantage under the tested budget, but do not uniquely identify the proposed causal mechanism.

Comparisons do not fully isolate the sources of improvement. Track2Act uses pooled ResNet18 features while the proposed model uses DINOv2 patch features and cross-attention. A matched-conditioning baseline and a deterministic version of the proposed architecture would better separate gains from representation, scene coverage, and stochastic modeling. The 'trained from scratch' framing also needs qualification because the image encoder is pretrained.

Physical plausibility and uncertainty are only partially validated. Low-rank trajectory structure is not sufficient to establish rigidity or correct collisions and dynamics. FVMD summarizes motion statistics, and best-of-K does not establish calibrated probabilities or comprehensive mode coverage. The synthetic evaluation contains only 16 initial scenes per split, with no confidence intervals or repeated-training analysis.

Several numerical inconsistencies need resolution. Table 13 reports an in-distribution FVMD of 6470.3 for Ours (L), versus 13745 in Table 3, without explaining the difference. The statement that all metrics worsen out of distribution contradicts several entries in Tables 3–4. These discrepancies reduce confidence in the evaluation's reproducibility.

Real-world evidence is mixed: Physics101 improves only modestly overall, and Table 16 reveals that the headline result uses the variant without the proposed VAE; the VAE variant performs worse than WAN overall. This distinction should be explicit in the main results. Together with the evaluation limitations, it prevents a stronger acceptance recommendation.
